questions.stem: When educating average-risk patients about how common dense breasts are, which NCI figure should you use?

choices.text: Dense breasts are rare — under 5% of screened women.
choices.rationale: NCI says nearly half of women 40+ who get mammograms have dense tissue.

choices.text: Only women with a BRCA variant have dense breasts.
choices.rationale: Density is common and not limited to genetic high-risk groups.

choices.text: Nearly half of women age 40 and older who get mammograms are found to have dense breast tissue.
choices.rationale: Correct. NCI: nearly half of screened women ≥40 have dense tissue.

choices.text: Density disappears after menopause for almost everyone.
choices.rationale: NCI does not teach that density vanishes for almost everyone after menopause.

questions.stem: Which presentation feature of inflammatory breast cancer is emphasized in this module’s dictionary-level evidence?

choices.text: It always presents as a painless, mobile, well-defined lump.
choices.rationale: That pattern fits common benign masses such as fibroadenoma, not IBC’s framing here.

choices.text: It is slow-growing and confined to a single milk duct without skin change.
choices.rationale: IBC is framed as rare, fast-growing, with skin lymph-vessel blockage.

choices.text: It often has no palpable lump, may not be seen on mammogram, and can show swollen/inflamed skin (including peau d’orange-like changes).
choices.rationale: Correct. Dictionary evidence: often no lump; skin inflammation; may be mammographically occult.

choices.text: It is defined solely by calcifications without clinical skin findings.
choices.rationale: IBC framing centers clinical skin/lymph findings, not calcifications alone.

questions.explanation: Inflammatory breast cancer is rare and fast-growing; cells block skin lymph vessels, causing swollen/inflamed appearance; often no palpable lump and may not be seen on mammogram; peau d’orange-like changes.

variants.simpler: IBC: inflamed/swollen skin, often no lump, may miss on mammogram.
variants.example: Document skin erythema/edema/peau d’orange even when no discrete mass is felt.

questions.stem: In plain language suitable for patient education, what is the sentinel lymph node?

choices.text: Any axillary node that looks fatty on mammography.
choices.rationale: Sentinel status is about drainage order from the tumor, not mammographic fat appearance.

choices.text: Every lymph node removed during a modified radical mastectomy.
choices.rationale: That describes a larger axillary dissection, not the sentinel definition.

choices.text: A benign intramammary node that never communicates with axillary pathways.
choices.rationale: Intramammary nodes are a different anatomy topic; sentinel means first drainage node.

choices.text: The first lymph node to which cancer is likely to spread from the primary tumor.
choices.rationale: Correct. Dictionary: first node likely to receive spread from the primary.

questions.explanation: The sentinel lymph node is the first lymph node to which cancer is likely to spread from the primary tumor.

variants.simpler: Sentinel node = first drainage node from the tumor.
variants.example: When a patient hears “sentinel node biopsy,” this is the definition to use.

questions.stem: A patient calls after a callback letter and says she is sure the letter means she has cancer. Which NCI-supported response is accurate without dismissing her fear?

choices.text: Callback letters are issued only after biopsy-proven malignancy.
choices.rationale: Callbacks request more imaging/biopsy workup; most are not cancer.

choices.text: Being called back can be frightening, but most people called back are not found to have breast cancer.
choices.rationale: Correct. NCI: most callbacks are not cancer.

choices.text: Any callback automatically upgrades the exam to Highly Suggestive of Malignancy.
choices.rationale: Callback ≠ that final assessment category.

choices.text: Technologists may tell her the radiologist already confirmed cancer on the screening images.
choices.rationale: Technologists must not invent a cancer diagnosis.

questions.explanation: NCI notes callbacks can be frightening, but most people who are called back are not found to have breast cancer.

variants.simpler: Most callbacks are not cancer — acknowledge fear, share that NCI fact.
variants.example: Use this reassurance while still directing her to complete the recommended follow-up.
